passage:
Sunday, week one. Usha's phone showed Imran's last message from nine days ago, a photo of his hostel mess dinner. She had not replied either. She felt a small ache and put the phone face down.

Thursday, week three. Usha stopped waiting for him to text first and sent a voice note: "Saw a dog that looks exactly like the one outside your old gate. Hope engineering is not eating you alive 🙂." No question, no "why so silent".

Saturday, week six. Imran answered at midnight with a long message about his new lab partner and a bad exam. They talked for twenty minutes. It was nothing like school, when they met every day, and Usha noticed she no longer expected it to be. She put a call in her diary for the first Sunday of each month and left the rest loose.

qa.q: What did Usha send when she stopped waiting for Imran to text first?
qa.a: She sent a voice note about a dog that looks exactly like the one outside his old gate, with no complaint in it.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she put the phone face down?
qa.a: A quiet sense of loss. The passage says she felt a small ache, and she set the phone down instead of firing off a message.

qa.q: What is worth copying in how Usha handled the distance?
qa.a: She reached out lightly without keeping score, and later set a monthly call, which keeps the friendship going without expecting it to match their school days.

qa.q: How might Imran have taken Usha's voice note after all those silent days?
qa.a: Probably as an easy, warm way back in. With no blame in it, he could reply without feeling guilty, which fits his long midnight reply.

grounding: Two friends in different cities drift apart; Usha feels the quiet loss, reaches out without scorekeeping, and lets the friendship become smaller.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,

I'm writing instead of calling because I didn't want to catch you at a bad moment. Since the semester began you have skipped our Sunday tea, and your replies take two days, sometimes just one word. I keep replaying the last few weeks, wondering if I said something wrong. 😔

So I'm asking once, and you can answer however you like, or not at all: is anything about us bothering you? If you are only busy or need some room, that is fine, truly. I will still be glad to hear about your day whenever you feel like telling me. There is no hurry to reply, and no need to explain more than you want to.

Your friend,
Vandana

qa.q: How long do Madhuri's replies take, according to Vandana?
qa.a: They take two days, and sometimes they are just one word.

qa.q: What is Vandana worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Vandana worries about having said something wrong, and admits to replaying the last few weeks over and over.

qa.q: What would you advise Vandana to do if Madhuri says they simply need space?
qa.a: Accept it kindly, stop asking, and stay warm without pressing for equal effort or a quick answer.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved that there is no blame and no pressure to answer fast, though they may also feel a little guilty. 🙂

grounding: A friend pulls back and Vandana wonders what went wrong, asks once kindly and offers space.

passage:
Sit, beta, and stop staring at your phone like that. I'm Zubin, and I once stared at mine exactly so.

In my second year of college my best friend Afreen started eating lunch with people from her theatre club. She laughed with them in a way I hadn't heard in years, and I felt hot behind my eyes. For a month I told myself I was fine. Once I even thought of "forgetting" to pass on a message about their rehearsal. I didn't.

One evening I said it plainly: "I miss you, and I'm hurt. That's mine to deal with, not yours." She went quiet, then hugged me. She still came to our chai stall on Fridays, and now she brought two of the theatre lot along. One of them is your aunt.

qa.q: Where did Zubin and Afreen still meet on Fridays?
qa.a: At their chai stall.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he watched Afreen laugh with her new group?
qa.a: Hurt. He says he felt hot behind his eyes and spent a month telling himself he was fine.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that helped, and what did he avoid?
qa.a: He said his hurt plainly to Afreen, and he did not go through with "forgetting" to pass on the rehearsal message.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt hearing Zubin's words?
qa.a: Probably surprised and touched, since she may not have noticed the distance. Her hug suggests she took it kindly.

grounding: Zubin, hurt at feeling replaced by his friend's new group, admits it plainly instead of sabotaging, and the friendship grows to include them.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Jomon, second year, asked to see me after the class group chat blew up over unkind messages about a batchmate, posted by his friend Avni. Several classmates now avoid her. Jomon said he has kept sitting with her at meals, and that it has cost him a few invitations.

He was clear on one point: he would not tell the warden the messages were not hers. "She did it. I told her it was cruel and that she owes an apology." He looked tired, not proud, and twice said he still likes her.

I did not tell him what to do. I asked what he wanted Avni to hear from him. "That I'm not leaving, and that this was wrong."

I have asked Avni to come in tomorrow, and I will check in with the batchmate too.

qa.q: What would Jomon not tell the warden?
qa.a: That the messages were not Avni's.

qa.q: What does Jomon seem to want, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He wants to keep the friendship while staying honest. He keeps sitting with Avni yet says her messages were cruel, and he looks tired rather than proud.

qa.q: What could the counsellor do next to support everyone involved?
qa.a: Meet Avni about making an apology, and check in with the batchmate who was targeted, as the note plans.

qa.q: How might the batchmate see the messages and Jomon's stance?
qa.a: They were probably hurt and left out by the messages, so hearing that someone called them wrong could matter to them.

grounding: Jomon stays loyal to Avni while refusing to cover her harmful behaviour.

passage:
Salma: Liz, that thing in the lab today. You didn't have to say all that to Rohan.
Elizabeth: He was blaming you for the group report and you did half of it. Somebody had to say it.
Salma: My hands were shaking. I couldn't get one word out.
Elizabeth: I saw. It's okay 🙂
Salma: Thank you. Really. 🤍 I'll borrow your notes and NOT lose them, promise.
Elizabeth: you lost them once lol
Salma: ONCE. Fine. Let me buy you chai on Friday, and when you present next week I'm sitting in the front row.
Elizabeth: Deal 😊
Salma: And if anyone ever talks over you, I'm the loud one this time.

qa.q: What had Rohan blamed Salma for?
qa.a: The group report. Elizabeth says Salma did half of it.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling in the lab, according to the chat?
qa.a: Frozen and anxious. Her hands were shaking and she couldn't get one word out.

qa.q: How does Salma show she isn't taking Elizabeth's help for granted?
qa.a: She thanks her, offers chai on Friday, promises to sit in the front row for Elizabeth's presentation, and says she will speak up for her next time.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Elizabeth to speak up in front of the lab?
qa.a: Probably nerve-racking, though she plays it down in the chat. She likely wanted Salma to feel backed up rather than alone with the blame. 🤍

grounding: A friend stands up for Salma in a hard moment and Salma answers with gratitude and a way to return it.

passage:
Eleven of them had squeezed into the back of a tempo to reach the Shivratri fair, shouting over a film song. Minakshi laughed when they laughed and held the bag of roasted peanuts, but nobody had asked why she'd gone quiet since her brother left for Pune. Near the jalebi stall she felt like a lamp lit in the daytime, there but not needed.

She could have slipped off to the bus stand. She had done it before, and no one had noticed. Instead she touched Bhavna's sleeve. "Come and look at bangles with me?"

Between the glass bangles she said, "I miss home even though I'm at home. It's strange." Bhavna stopped bargaining. "I'll tell the others we'll be late," she said, and then simply listened, holding a green bangle she never bought.

qa.q: How many friends squeezed into the tempo?
qa.a: Eleven of them.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel unseen among her friends?
qa.a: Nobody had asked why she had gone quiet since her brother left for Pune, so she felt like a lamp lit in the daytime, there but not needed.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's choice at the fair differ from slipping away to the bus stand?
qa.a: She told one friend something real, so she was no longer alone with it. Slipping away would have left everyone unaware.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have felt when Minakshi said this?
qa.a: Probably surprise and care. Stopping her bargaining and offering to tell the others they would be late suggests she took it seriously.

grounding: Among many friends Minakshi feels unseen and shares something real with one person instead of withdrawing.

subtype: Friend × Being the one who always reaches out [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Vaibhav counted: he had called Indu three times, planned the birthday dinner and booked the table. She had answered with "sure 👍" and nothing else. His jaw tightened. He typed a long message about effort, then deleted it.

The next Sunday, he decided to plan nothing for ten days and simply see what happened. He didn't tell Indu and he didn't sulk. Ten days went by with two memes from her and no plans.

Two Fridays later he called. "I noticed I'm always the one who calls. Is that because it's hard for you, or because you'd rather not?" Indu was quiet, then said her new job left her flat by evening and she'd assumed he liked organising. She offered to plan the next one herself. He said he'd like that, and that he would still call sometimes, just not every time.

qa.q: What did Indu answer when Vaibhav planned the birthday dinner?
qa.a: She answered with "sure" and a thumbs-up, and nothing else.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he deleted his long message, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Resentful. His jaw tightened, and he wrote about effort but did not send it, perhaps to avoid a blurt of anger.

qa.q: Why was it useful for Vaibhav to step back for ten days before speaking?
qa.a: It showed him what happened when he did not organise anything, so he could ask from facts rather than from silent resentment.

qa.q: How did Indu see the pattern before Vaibhav asked?
qa.a: She assumed he liked organising, and her new job left her flat by evening, so she had not realised it felt one-sided to him.

grounding: Vaibhav does all the reaching out, steps back once to see the truth, then speaks honestly and decides what the friendship deserves.

subtype: Friend × Old friend and new self [Actor]
passage:
The receptionist at the design studio buzzed. "Afreen, a friend called Jagdish is here." Afreen, halfway through her internship review, felt her stomach drop.

Jagdish stood in the lobby holding a paper bag of the same samosas from outside their school gate. "You look different," he grinned. "You look exactly the same," she said, warmer than it sounded.

She had planned to duck out and say she was busy. Instead she introduced him to her supervisor as "my friend from Class Six" and took her break early. On the steps they ate. He asked one thing about typography; she asked how his cousin's shop was doing. Then they laughed about Mr Sharma's chalk-throwing.

"I never know what to say about my work to you," she admitted. Jagdish shrugged. "Say a little. I'll nod."

qa.q: What did Jagdish bring to the studio?
qa.a: A paper bag of the same samosas from outside their school gate.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel on hearing Jagdish was in the lobby, and what had she first planned?
qa.a: A jolt of nervousness. She had planned to duck out and say she was busy.

qa.q: What does introducing Jagdish as "my friend from Class Six" do well?
qa.a: It honours their shared history openly, and she neither hides him nor hides her new working life.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see it when Afreen says she never knows what to say about her work?
qa.a: Probably as honest rather than snobbish. His answer, "Say a little. I'll nod," suggests he would rather have her open than pretend nothing has changed.

grounding: Afreen has grown while her school friend has not, and she honours the shared history while accepting they have less in common.

passage:
I'm Minakshi, and being in the middle is funny. Everyone is very nice to you, right until they aren't.

Last term Bhavna and Deepa stopped speaking over a borrowed laptop charger, or really over what the charger meant. Bhavna sat on my bed one night and said, "You saw how she treated me, right?" The next day Deepa cornered me: "Tell me what she said about me." My stomach twisted, because part of me wanted to please whoever was in the room.

I told each of them the same thing. "I won't carry messages. I care about you both, and honestly the charger seems small next to the friendship, but I'm not going to pick a side." Bhavna stormed off. Deepa called me useless. It hurt 😔.

A month later they each told me, separately, that they trusted me because I never repeated what they'd said.

qa.q: What did Bhavna and Deepa stop speaking over?
qa.a: A borrowed laptop charger, or really what the charger meant.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's stomach twist when each friend asked her to take a side?
qa.a: Part of her wanted to please whoever was in the room, even though she knew she should not carry tales.

qa.q: What could someone in Minakshi's position say when both friends want them on their side?
qa.a: Say kindly that they will not carry messages or pick a side, keep their own view, and stay warm to both.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna and Deepa have trusted Minakshi later?
qa.a: Because she never repeated what either had said, each could tell she would not repeat their words to others either.

grounding: Two friends fall out and both want Minakshi on their side; she refuses to carry tales and stays kind to both.

passage:
Zeenat's message came in while I was doing laundry. "Can you spare some for the mess bill again? Will return, promise." My name is Tanuja, and that word "again" sat in my stomach. Last time she promised too. I hadn't minded the money as much as the pretending: I'd smiled at her, then complained about her to my roommate.

This time I sat on my bunk and worked out what I could give without skipping my own bus pass. I wrote back, "I can give a small amount, and please treat it as a gift, not a loan. That's my limit for now."

She sent a heart, and later, "thanks for being straight." I felt lighter, though a bit anxious that she might feel judged. I still don't know if she'll ask again.

qa.q: What did Zeenat ask for money to cover?
qa.a: The mess bill.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling about Zeenat's message, and why?
qa.a: Uneasy and a little resentful. The word "again" sat in her stomach, and she had already complained about Zeenat to her roommate.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that protected both her limits and the friendship?
qa.a: She gave only what she could as a gift, said plainly that it was her limit, and did not pretend she had nothing.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt on receiving the reply?
qa.a: Possibly embarrassed or judged at first. Her heart and "thanks for being straight" suggest relief at an honest answer.

grounding: A friend asks for a loan again; Tanuja gives within her means as a gift and states her limit honestly.
